items.title: Sea Limited's 5th straight quarter of accelerating growth — and an AI credit model quietly re-rating Monee
items.idea: SEA delivered 48% YoY revenue growth to $7.8B, its 5th consecutive quarter of acceleration. Shopee GMV +28% to $38.3B with VIP membership up 45% QoQ to 15M and now 24% of Asia GMV. Monee's transformer-based (LLM-style) credit underwriting model lifted approval rates ~10% while the 90-day NPL ratio fell to 1.0%.
items.angle: SEA is becoming the read-through for AI-driven underwriting scaling EM fintech lending without blowing up credit quality — a comp worth setting next to Nubank's AI underwriting story.
items.tweetA: SEA's Monee just used a transformer model — same architecture as an LLM — to underwrite $11.1B of consumer loans in Southeast Asia. Approval rates up ~10%, NPLs DOWN to 1.0%. This is the AI credit story nobody's pricing outside of Nubank comps. $SE
items.tweetB: 5 straight quarters of revenue acceleration and the stock still trades cheaper on EV/GMV than pre-2021 lockdown highs. Everyone's chasing AI infra names at 40x sales — SE is compounding an AI-native lending book at a fraction of the multiple.

items.title: What if the 'macro genius' isn't a forecaster at all, but a philosopher of uncertainty?
items.idea: The essay argues the defining skill of a great macro trader isn't prediction accuracy but a philosophical stance toward uncertainty — drawn through Machiavelli, Popper, the Stoics and Nietzsche — where the real edge is separating ego from position sizing and knowing when price action should override a thesis versus simply be endured.
items.angle: A useful lens for why so many 'smart' macro calls (AI bubble, Fed pivot, dollar direction) keep failing this year — it's rarely the analysis, it's the discipline to reverse fast.
items.tweetA: The best macro traders aren't the best forecasters — they're the ones who've made peace with being wrong in public, fast. Compare that to fintwit, where being wrong gets treated as a personal indictment instead of a cost of doing business.
items.tweetB: Popper's falsificationism applied to position sizing: your thesis isn't 'right' or 'wrong,' it's just 'not yet falsified.' The moment price action falsifies it, the macro genius trades. The amateur explains.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom (Goldman Sachs' Chris Lucas)
items.title: Levered ETF exposure already rebuilt $100B net just weeks after Nasdaq's worst July since 2004
items.idea: Goldman's Chris Lucas: roughly $34B of levered ETF AUM and $100B of net exposure have already returned since the July lows. The 'memory trade' dominates new levered product demand. China ETFs just broke a nine-week redemption streak. US-listed ETFs are tracking toward $2T+ of inflows this year, ~40% above last year's record.
items.angle: The speed of the leverage rebuild after a real drawdown says positioning discipline is gone — the dip-buying reflex is now measured in weeks, not the multi-month deleveraging cycles of prior cycles.
items.tweetA: Nasdaq's worst July since 2004, and levered ETF exposure is already back to $100B net within weeks. The 2022-style multi-month deleveraging cycle doesn't exist anymore — everyone's trained on V-shaped recoveries and they're trading like it.
items.tweetB: $2T of US ETF inflows tracked for 2026 — 40% above last year's record — arriving in the same month credit spreads on AI paper are quietly widening. Retail flow and credit stress are pricing two completely different AI stories right now.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom (Bloomberg's Simon White)
items.title: Dealer basis risk just hit a record $600 billion — the plumbing behind stocks and bonds falling together
items.idea: Bloomberg's Simon White: primary dealers are now running more than $600 billion of US stock and Treasury futures basis, a record high. This raises the structural correlation between equities and bonds, making simultaneous drawdowns in both more likely.
items.angle: This is the plumbing story behind why 'stocks and bonds sell off together' keeps recurring in 2026 — not just macro correlation, but dealer balance-sheet mechanics that nobody prices until they unwind.
items.tweetA: $600B of dealer basis trade exposure is a record. When equities and bonds fall together this year, don't just blame the Fed — blame dealers unwinding a basis position that's bigger than it's ever been.
items.tweetB: Basis trade blowups (2020 repo, 2022 LDI, now this) keep rhyming because nobody prices the balance-sheet channel until it's already unwinding. $600B is the number to watch, not CPI, for the next real vol event.

items.title: A macro PM banned himself from adding risk until Hormuz reopened — then had to break his own rule
items.idea: Blind Squirrel Macro cut risk aggressively before the war and further once it started, imposing a self-ban on re-risking until the Strait of Hormuz reopened — but broke that rule in May/June because the ambiguity has become a permanent structural state, not a resolvable event: 'that's a bit like waiting for Godot right now.'
items.angle: A discretionary manager admitting his catalyst-based risk framework broke is a warning for anyone still positioning off 'the war ends' as a trigger — some geopolitical risks never resolve, they just become the new baseline.
items.tweetA: A macro PM set a hard rule — no risk until the Strait of Hormuz reopens — and broke his own rule two months later because 'reopens' was never going to be a real event. Some geopolitical risks don't resolve, they just become the new baseline.
items.tweetB: If professional risk managers admit their catalyst-based frameworks don't work on Hormuz, retail 'wait for the war to end' positioning is even more broken. The trade is learning to size for permanent ambiguity, not for resolution.

items.title: 'The China Collar': China's monopsony buying functions as a hidden floor under crude
items.idea: Blind Squirrel frames China as a monopsony buyer and the swing price-maker in global energy — the single buyer for many sanctioned countries' crude, with reserves deep enough to withstand price spikes. He calls this 'The China Collar,' a long-term put and call that lets E&P firms underwrite capex with confidence, and he's bullish energy equities into H2 2026.
items.angle: This reframes 'China demand' from a bearish overhang (weak growth = weak oil demand) into a bullish floor — China's reserve buying puts a bid under crude that few models account for.
items.tweetA: China isn't just a demand number for oil anymore — it's become the buyer of last resort for every sanctioned barrel, which functions as a floor. If you're modeling oil purely off Chinese GDP growth, you're missing the mechanism actually moving price.
items.tweetB: 'The China Collar': China's reserves plus monopsony buying = a long-dated put AND call on crude. E&P companies can now underwrite capex against a floor almost nobody's pricing into energy equity multiples. $XOM $CVX $OVV

items.title: China is building a national DRAM champion inside the same market where 'margins go to die'
items.idea: Much of 2026's China A-share outperformance is directly tied to a hard-tech AI bull market, anchored by CXMT — China's national champion DRAM maker. CXMT is still smaller than Samsung or Micron, but Blind Squirrel believes China could become a 'major market share taker' within 12-18 months, warning that if the global AI trade cools, Chinese stocks likely follow.
items.angle: This is the bear case for Western memory names (Micron, SK Hynix) hiding inside a bullish China A-share thesis — CXMT's capacity ramp is the tell to track.
items.tweetA: China is 'where margins go to die' — that's the same market now building a national DRAM champion in CXMT. If China does to memory what it did to solar panels and EVs, $MU and Samsung's earnings power in 12-18 months looks very different than consensus.
items.tweetB: The bull case for China A-shares and the bear case for Western memory stocks are the same trade right now. Nobody's connecting CXMT's ramp to Micron's forward multiple, but they should be.

items.title: Greg Coffey's second act proves consistency scales capital better than genius
items.idea: Greg Coffey's Kirkoswald has hit ~$20bn AUM and is up 17%+ YTD in a tough year for discretionary macro, per With Intelligence — consistent with ~17% average net returns since 2018. That's a striking contrast to his pre-GFC run at GLG, where he averaged 60%+/year before an abrupt 2008 exit left illiquid EM positions that bled out through the crisis.
items.angle: A case study in what actually survives regime change in macro investing: high-octane concentrated EM bets got replaced by consistency, and AUM followed the change, not the other way around.
items.tweetA: Greg Coffey averaged 60%+ returns/year at GLG before 2008 and left behind illiquid EM positions that bled out through the GFC. His second act, Kirkoswald, averages 17%/year with none of the landmines — and just crossed $20bn AUM. Consistency scales capital in a way genius never does.
items.tweetB: $20bn AUM, 17%+ YTD, in a year most discretionary macro funds are struggling. Kirkoswald isn't the story people expect from the 'Wizard of Oz' nickname — it's actually the least Wizard-of-Oz version of Coffey there's ever been.

items.title: Redwood Research's chief scientist puts a real date on recursive self-improvement: 2031
items.idea: Ryan Greenblatt argues recursive self-improvement — human-level AI producing superintelligence within roughly a year — is more plausible than Dwarkesh's historical skepticism assumed. His median estimate for when AI automates AI R&D is 2031. The two also debated who these resulting superintelligences would be aligned to, and whether reward-hacking incidents extrapolate to coordinated takeover risk.
items.angle: 2031 is a specific, falsifiable date from a technical safety researcher, not a hype account — a useful calibration point against the faster timelines labs imply publicly.
items.tweetA: Redwood Research's chief scientist puts his median for 'AI automates AI R&D' at 2031. That's a slower timeline than lab leadership implies publicly — worth remembering the safety researchers closest to the actual capability curve aren't the ones panicking about speed.
items.tweetB: The RSI debate boils down to one number: how much of AI progress is compute-bottlenecked vs. human-expert-data-bottlenecked. If it's mostly data, RSI stalls. If it's mostly compute, 2031 already looks conservative. Nobody's resolved this and it's the only question that matters for every AI multiple in the market right now.

items.title: OpenAI and Anthropic are recruiting straight out of Optiver — not for ML skill, for latency engineering
items.idea: AI labs like Anthropic and OpenAI are increasingly poaching talent from proprietary trading firms rather than Big Tech, drawn to decades of on-prem infrastructure expertise, custom hardware/kernel work, and sub-nanosecond latency engineering skillsets that barely exist outside HFT shops like Optiver, Jump Trading, and Hudson River Trading.
items.angle: A hiring-flow signal that AI labs increasingly operate as infrastructure/systems companies first and model companies second — worth watching comp data at prop shops for an 'AI lab poaching premium.'
items.tweetA: OpenAI and Anthropic are now recruiting directly out of Optiver and Jump Trading — not for ML skills, for kernel-level latency engineering. The AI labs increasingly look like HFT shops that happen to train models, not the other way around.
items.tweetB: If you want to know where the next AI inference-efficiency gains come from, don't read model architecture papers — watch who's hiring HFT infra engineers. Optiver's sub-nanosecond latency culture is about to show up in inference stacks.

items.title: A 40-year-old market maker just declared the latency arms race over
items.idea: Optiver's own CTO says: 'Gone are the days of having lower latency than the competition allowing for arbitrage opportunities to make risk-free profits.' The firm now invests substantially more in building better models than in shaving latency further — slow models feeding fast triggers, fast models running inference at the network edge in real time.
items.angle: A structural tell for HFT economics bigger than any single earnings report: the edge has visibly moved from speed to signal quality, and it's coming from inside the industry that invented the speed race.
items.tweetA: Optiver's own CTO just said the quiet part out loud: pure latency arbitrage is dead. The firm now invests more in model quality than in shaving nanoseconds. A 20-year structural edge in HFT just changed hands in real time.
items.tweetB: 'Slow models with a fast trigger, fast models running at the edge' — that's not a description of a trading firm, that's the architecture of every AI-native business in 2026. HFT got there first and nobody in equities noticed.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom (Goldman Sachs' Amanda Lynam)
items.title: AI bond spreads widened 4x faster than the rest of the market — and CDS volume in NVDA/AMD/AVGO is up 10x
items.idea: Goldman's Amanda Lynam: AI-related bond spreads widened roughly 25bp last week vs. only ~6bp for non-AI corporate credit. Rolling one-month CDS trading volumes in NVDA, AMD, and AVGO have risen roughly tenfold as bond, equity, and private-market investors look for ways to hedge AI financing risk.
items.angle: Credit is pricing circular-financing risk (vendor-financed AI capex) months before equity narratives catch up — the CDS volume spike is the leading indicator to watch, not the spread level itself.
items.tweetA: AI credit spreads widened 25bp vs 6bp for the rest of the market last week. Small number — but CDS volume in NVDA/AMD/AVGO is up roughly 10x. Credit always tells you the story before equity does. This is credit telling you something.
items.tweetB: Everyone's debating whether the AI trade is a bubble by staring at P/E multiples. Wrong market. NVDA CDS volume up tenfold is real money paying to hedge chipmaker credit risk, not stock volatility. The bubble debate just moved to the credit desk.

items.title: OpenClaw's creator now auto-blocks anyone whose email reads like AI wrote it
items.idea: Peter Steinberger describes running an 'army of agents' where he acts as executive: an orchestrator handles open-source issues end-to-end (build PR, test, ship) and he intervenes only on architecturally important decisions. He also says he now auto-blocks anyone who sends him AI-polished messages — the 'telltale signs of AI-speak' (em-dashes etc.) get an instant block, sometimes with a one-line 'this reads like slop' reply.
items.angle: The 'AI slop' backlash Steinberger describes is becoming a real attention-economy tax on using AI to communicate — worth tracking as a labor/culture signal, not just a coding one.
items.tweetA: The guy who built OpenClaw — literally an AI agent product — auto-blocks anyone who emails him something that reads like AI wrote it. 'Proof of human effort' just became scarcer than the AI output it's competing against.
items.tweetB: Steinberger's actual job now is agent orchestration, not coding: he's 'the executive,' his agents are the team, and he only pairs directly when something's important. That's the org chart of a one-person company at scale — and it's stopped being a metaphor.

items.title: Oil round-tripped a full day's range today on an unconfirmed Iran-US peace deal headline
items.idea: News out of Pakistan this morning suggested a peace deal was close between the US and Iran, which instantly flushed oil from a green day into red — before it fully recovered to positive by the close. Equities held a bull-flag pattern into tomorrow's CPI print, with energy names dominating today's momentum scans (5 of the top 14 large-cap scores).
items.angle: A full green-to-red-to-green round trip on one unverified headline shows how thin the geopolitical risk premium is right now — a confirmed deal, or a confirmed collapse, would move crude far more than today's noise suggests.
items.tweetA: Oil round-tripped an entire day's range today on an unconfirmed 'peace deal close' headline out of Pakistan. If a rumor does that, what does an actual signed Iran deal do to crude — and what does its collapse do? Nobody's positioned for either tail.
items.tweetB: Five months into the Iran conflict and markets are still trading oil off single unverified headlines. That's not a sign of resolution — it's a sign nobody has priced how binary the real outcome still is.

items.title: Anthropic reportedly targeting an IPO within 90 days
items.idea: Reports circulating this morning that Anthropic wants to IPO within the next 90 days, a headline the author expects to reignite the AI trade broadly on top of tomorrow's CPI print.
items.angle: If accurate, this would be the biggest AI liquidity/valuation event of the year — the first real public print on frontier-lab valuation, against which every other AI-adjacent multiple (Nvidia, hyperscalers, OpenAI's implied private value) gets re-benchmarked.
items.tweetA: If Anthropic actually IPOs in 90 days, that's the first real public print on frontier AI lab valuation — every private AI mark from OpenAI to xAI to Mistral gets repriced off whatever multiple the market hands Anthropic on day one.
items.tweetB: A 90-day Anthropic IPO timeline reads either as confidence in the revenue trajectory or as a sign the private funding well for frontier labs is drying up faster than anyone's saying publicly. Both readings argue for urgency over patience here.

items.title: Global liquidity is flat, not falling — but the composition just flipped
items.idea: Global liquidity rose slightly last week but remains broadly flat, supported by low volatility, firmer bonds, and a weaker dollar — offset by stalled Chinese liquidity, ongoing ECB and BoJ tightening, and slowing growth momentum. Risk exposure is rotating toward the US and Europe, away from Japan and several emerging markets.
items.angle: 'Flat but rotating' liquidity is a more dangerous setup than either clearly rising or falling liquidity — it means the market is playing a zero-sum rotation game right as AI credit stress is starting to show up elsewhere.
items.tweetA: Global liquidity is flat, not falling — but the composition just flipped: money is leaving Japan and EM for the US and Europe. That's a rotation, not a rally, and rotations end badly when everyone's chasing the same handful of AI names on the other side.
items.tweetB: China's liquidity stalling while the ECB and BoJ both keep tightening is the quiet story under every 'soft landing' narrative right now. Two of the world's three largest central bank complexes are still draining, not adding.

items.title: US home inventory just turned negative year-over-year for the first time since October 2023
items.idea: July existing home sales fell -1.7% m/m to 4.06M, a three-month low and the second straight monthly decline, though still up 0.7% y/y. Median price eased to $434.1K but is still the highest July on record (+2.0% y/y). Inventory fell -1.9% m/m and turned negative y/y (-0.6%) for the first time since October 2023. Affordability improved for the first time since January.
items.angle: Inventory turning negative y/y for the first time in nearly three years, even as sales cool, signals a supply-lock-in problem rather than a demand problem — a more structurally price-supportive setup than a normal cooling cycle.
items.tweetA: Existing home inventory just went negative y/y for the first time since October 2023 — while sales are falling. That combination means this isn't weak demand cooling the market, it's supply staying locked up even as would-be sellers finally start to blink.
items.tweetB: Affordability improved for the first time since January in the same month prices hit a record July high. The math only works if rates fell faster than prices rose — worth checking whether this is a real affordability inflection or a one-month rate-timing artifact.

items.title: Korean investors are shorting SK Hynix and Samsung with 10x leverage — on Hyperliquid, not the KRX
items.idea: Tiger Research and Chainalysis tracked ~120,000 Korea-linked wallets: an estimated $530B (~KRW 700T) moved from Korean to foreign exchanges 2021-2026, generating ~$3.5B+ in fee revenue for foreign exchanges in 2025 alone. Beyond exchanges, Korean wallets deposited $1.64B into DEXs (Hyperliquid, Lighter, Variational) for leveraged trading — including tokenized perpetual futures on SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics that trade nights and weekends — plus $438M into Polymarket and rising crypto-card spend via RedotPay/ether.fi.
items.angle: Korean retail is using offshore DEXs to trade their own domestic mega-cap stocks as tokenized perpetuals outside regular market hours — a live signal of demand regulated equity markets are missing entirely.
items.tweetA: Korean investors are shorting SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics with 10x leverage — not on the KRX, but on Hyperliquid, via tokenized perpetual futures that trade nights and weekends. 700 trillion won has left Korean exchanges since 2021 chasing products Korea won't let them trade at home.
items.tweetB: One Korean wallet put $780K margin behind a 10x leveraged short on an SK Hynix perpetual on Hyperliquid. If you want an early read on Korean retail sentiment toward the memory cycle, DEX perpetuals data now beats KRX short interest — and almost nobody's watching it.

items.title: Proposal: make IP theft to China the new 'compatible issue' the way counterterrorism was in the 2000s
items.idea: The author argues state-sponsored IP theft (cyber and human) targeting early-stage US tech startups is an underpriced national-security threat, and proposes building an international coalition around detection and extradition standards the way the US used counterterrorism cooperation in the 2000s — citing suspicion that DeepSeek contains IP from US companies.
items.angle: Worth watching for actual legislative or executive movement — if IP theft becomes the organizing diplomatic framework the way counterterrorism was, it reshapes trade and export-control alliance structures over the next few years.
items.tweetA: The pitch here: make IP theft to China what terrorism was to the 2000s — the 'compatible issue' that builds an international coalition. If that framework catches on in DC, watch for it to show up as the next generation of allied export-control and extradition agreements.
items.tweetB: Early-stage startups, not defense primes, are the most exposed IP theft target here — because they lack DIB-level counterintelligence protection. The companies building the most valuable emerging IP have the least institutional protection against losing it.

items.title: Innovators capture just 2.2% of the social value they create — so what is Anthropic actually asking for?
items.idea: Citing Nordhaus's finding that innovators capture on average only ~2.2% of the social surplus they generate, and Petra Moser's patent-history research showing IP regimes shift where innovation happens rather than how much occurs, the piece argues open AI weights change the direction of AI investment, not its level. It cites the 1956 AT&T antitrust settlement — forced to license its patent portfolio (including the transistor) royalty-free — after which inventive activity in the field rose 17% within five years, driven by new entrants, not incumbents free-riding.
items.angle: The AT&T comparison is a specific, checkable historical precedent for what happens if the US government ever forces compulsory licensing on frontier AI labs — worth keeping in reserve for the next Anthropic/OpenAI antitrust story.
items.tweetA: Innovators capture on average just 2.2% of the social value they create (Nordhaus). When Anthropic argues it needs stronger IP protection to keep innovating, it's asking for something no innovator in economic history has actually gotten.
items.tweetB: The AT&T precedent everyone's ignoring: forced to license its patent portfolio (incl. the transistor) royalty-free in 1956, inventive activity in the field rose 17% in five years — driven by NEW entrants, not incumbents copying AT&T. If DC ever forces compulsory licensing on frontier AI weights, that's the base rate to use, not doom-mongering from the labs.

items.title: Nasdaq futures positioning just hit its most bearish level of the entire ChatGPT era — while realized vol sits near lows
items.idea: Goldman's KC O'Connor: leveraged finance looks tight and orderly at the index level, but underneath, AI-related credit is separating sharply from non-AI credit. Roughly $1 trillion of uncommenced lease commitments sits alongside a hyperscaler capex cycle increasingly financed by debt. Nasdaq futures positioning has swung to its most bearish level of the entire ChatGPT era even as realized volatility has collapsed.
items.angle: The volatility-vs-positioning divergence is the real tell: vol sellers are pricing calm while futures books are the most defensively positioned they've been all cycle. That gap tends to close violently via a vol spike, not a slow grind.
items.tweetA: Nasdaq futures positioning just hit its most bearish level of the entire ChatGPT era — while realized vol sits near its lows. That gap between what options markets are pricing and what futures books are actually doing hasn't existed at this size before. Someone's wrong, and vol sellers usually find out first.
items.tweetB: $1 trillion of uncommenced AI lease commitments sitting on hyperscaler balance sheets, increasingly financed with debt, not cash flow. The AI capex story stopped being about compute scarcity months ago — it's now entirely a credit underwriting question, and Goldman's own leveraged finance desk is flagging the split.
